name: L-Carnitine

lead: L-carnitine is a compound synthesised in the liver and kidneys from lysine and methionine and obtained from foods such as red meat. It is sold as a supplement, often in the forms L-carnitine tartrate or acetyl-L-carnitine, for fat loss, exercise recovery and energy.
Its physiological role is well established, but supplementation in people who are not deficient has produced modest and inconsistent effects on weight and body composition across meta-analyses.

paras: Carnitine carries long-chain fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane so they can be oxidised for energy, and it buffers excess acetyl groups. Oral supplementation raises plasma levels but does not reliably raise muscle carnitine in healthy people without additional measures, which may explain the weak results.

Intakes of about 2 to 3 g daily are generally tolerated, with nausea, diarrhoea and a fishy body odour at higher intakes. Gut bacteria convert carnitine to trimethylamine, which the liver turns into TMAO, a compound associated with cardiovascular risk in observational studies, though causality is unresolved. It is sold as a supplement and is unscheduled in most places.

lead: L-Carnitine is the biologically active form of carnitine, a quaternary ammonium compound derived from amino acids that carries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria so they can be oxidised for energy. It is concentrated in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Healthy people, including strict vegetarians, generally make enough of it in the body, and it was first extracted from meat in 1905, which gave it its name from the Latin for flesh.[1]

It is sold as a supplement in oral, liquid and injectable forms and is used by athletes and dieters for fat loss, exercise performance and recovery. Wikipedia states that the quality of clinical research for these uses has been low, preventing firm conclusions.[1] A 2020 meta-analysis of 37 randomized trials with 2,292 participants reported small average reductions in body weight, body mass index and fat mass.[2]

Intake of carnitine has also been the subject of research on gut-bacteria-derived trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a compound that has been linked in observational and animal work to cardiovascular risk.[3]
infobox: Oral; injected forms are also discussed in forums
About 20 g in a 70 kg adult, mostly in muscle [1]
Dietary supplement; prescription forms exist for deficiency states

paras: Because carnitine transports fatty acids into mitochondria, supplements are promoted for fat loss and for exercise performance and recovery. T Nation users list it in pre-workout stacks, in competition-prep supplement lists and, in some posts, as an injected product; others describe it as helpful during thyroid-related fatigue or ask about it as a general aid.[4][5][6][7][8]
Wikipedia notes that athletes commonly take it for performance and recovery despite insufficient high-quality evidence of benefit.[1]

Carnitine supplementation is used for primary carnitine deficiency, a genetic transporter disorder, and for secondary deficiencies such as those occurring in chronic kidney disease and in preterm infants.[1] Trials have also examined it in conditions such as diabetic kidney disease, spinal muscular atrophy (with valproic acid), cancer-related fatigue and pressure ulcers, with guideline bodies reaching their own conclusions in each setting.[9][10][11][12]

The 2020 dose-response meta-analysis of 37 randomized trials reported that carnitine supplementation reduced body weight by about 1.2 kg on average, BMI by about 0.24 kg/m2 and fat mass by about 2.1 kg, with no significant effect on waist circumference or body-fat percentage; restricting the analysis to high-quality trials confirmed only the weight effect, and the dose-response relationship was non-linear.[2][13]

For exercise, a 2018 review concluded that carnitine has been investigated as an ergogenic aid, that early work suggested effects on maximal oxygen uptake and power, and that later studies point to benefits for recovery such as reduced muscle soreness and markers of muscle damage, with potential effects on muscle mass in older adults.[14] A 2021 trial of carnitine tartrate for five weeks in men and women examined exercise recovery.[15] Wikipedia cites a 2021 systematic review that found carnitine may improve high-intensity performance and recovery but described results as inconclusive because regimens varied, and reports no consistent effect at moderate intensity.[1]

A 2024 meta-analysis addressed carnitine's effect on lipid profile in adults.[16] A 2023 randomized crossover study found that caffeine increased the clearance of carnitine from plasma.[17] Registered trials have examined skeletal muscle mass, among many other conditions.[18]

In 2013 a Nature Medicine study reported that gut microbes metabolise dietary L-carnitine into trimethylamine, which the liver converts to TMAO, and that this pathway promoted atherosclerosis in mice and was associated with cardiovascular risk in people.[3] Follow-up work examined TMAO in kidney disease and stroke populations, and a 2022 trial in hemodialysis patients tested whether a dietary fiber could lower TMAO.[19][20][21] The significance of supplemental carnitine for cardiovascular risk in people has therefore been an active research question.
The D-form of carnitine is described as toxic because it inhibits the activity of the L-form.[1]

Carnitine acyltransferases move long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation. The entry step is a rate-limiting control point for fat oxidation and is inhibited by malonyl-CoA when the liver is making fat and relieved when AMPK activation lowers malonyl-CoA during fasting or vigorous contraction.[1] Carnitine also buffers acetyl-CoA levels, removes acyl groups as acylcarnitines and has antioxidant activity.[1][22]

Adults on mixed diets take in roughly 60 to 180 mg a day from food, compared with about 10 to 12 mg for vegans, and the body synthesises roughly 11 to 34 mg daily. Between 54 and 86 percent of dietary carnitine is absorbed. Supplemental carnitine has a plasma half-life of about 17 hours, and uptake into tissue depends on the OCTN2 transporter.[1][23]

In forum logs carnitine appears most often as one item among many supplements taken before training, including citrulline, beta-alanine and betaine, and in some cases alongside testosterone and growth hormone. Mentions of injectable carnitine appear in posts by users on testosterone replacement.[5][6][7][8][24]

lore.intro: In strength-sport communities carnitine is treated as a routine pre-workout or fat-loss supplement, and some users inject it.[5][6][7]
